text: India is located north of the equator, stretching from 8°4' north to 37°6' north latitude and from 68°7' east to 97°25' east longitude. It is the seventh-largest country in the world, covering a total area of 3,287,263 square kilometres (1,269,219 mi²), measuring 3,214 km (1,997 mi) from north to south and 2,933 km (1,822 mi) from east to west. India has a land frontier of 15,200 km (9,445 mi) and a coastline of 7,516.6 km (4,671 mi). It extends into the Indian Ocean, bordered by the Arabian Sea to the west, the Lakshadweep Sea to the southwest, the Bay of Bengal to the east, and the Indian Ocean proper to the south. The Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar separate India from Sri Lanka to its southeast, and the Maldives are 125 km (78 mi) south of India's Lakshadweep Islands across the Eight Degree Channel. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands, 1,200 km (750 mi) southeast of the mainland, share maritime borders with Myanmar, Thailand, and Indonesia. The southernmost tip of the Indian mainland is just south of Kanyakumari at 8°4′38″N, 77°31′56″E, while the southernmost point in India is Indira Point on Great Nicobar Island. The northernmost point under Indian administration is Indira Col in the Siachen Glacier. India's territorial waters extend 12 nautical miles (13.8 mi; 22.2 km) from the coast baseline, and it has the 18th largest Exclusive Economic Zone of 2,305,143 km² (890,021 mi²). The northern frontier is defined by the Himalayan mountain range, where India borders China, Bhutan, and Nepal; its western border with Pakistan runs through the Karakoram and Western Himalayan ranges, the Punjab Plains, the Thar Desert, and the Rann of Kutch, covering 3,323 km (2,065 mi) and passing through Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Gujarat. A Line of Control (LoC) serves as an informal boundary between Indian and Pakistan-administered Kashmir areas, with India claiming the entire former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, including areas currently administered by Pakistan and China. The border with Bangladesh is 4,096.70 km (2,545.57 mi) long, shared by West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram; before 2015, there were 92 Bangladeshi enclaves in India and 106 Indian enclaves in Bangladesh, which were exchanged to simplify the border, resulting in India losing approximately 40 km² (9,900 acres) to Bangladesh. The Line of Actual Control (LAC) marks the effective border between India and China, spanning 4,057 km through Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Arunachal Pradesh. The border with Myanmar extends 1,643 km (1,021 mi) along the northeastern states of Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram. India's border with Bhutan is 699 km (434 mi) long, shared by Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam, and Arunachal Pradesh, while the border with Nepal is 1,751 km (1,088 mi) long, running along the Himalayan foothills in northern India through Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, and Sikkim. The Siliguri Corridor, narrowed by borders with Bhutan, Nepal, and Bangladesh, connects peninsular India with the northeastern states. India is divided into 28 states and 8 union territories, including the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The country's borders run a total length of 15,200 km (9,400 mi). The borders with Pakistan and Bangladesh were established by the Radcliffe Line in 1947 during the Partition of India. The Ganges is the longest river originating in India, and the Ganges–Brahmaputra system covers most of northern, central, and eastern India, while the Deccan Plateau occupies most of southern India. Kangchenjunga in Sikkim is the highest point in India at 8,586 m (28,169 ft), the world's third highest peak. India's climate ranges from equatorial in the far south to alpine and tundra in the upper Himalayas. Geologically, India lies on the Indian Plate, a major tectonic plate that split from the ancient continent Gondwanaland. The Indo-Australian Plate is divided into the Indian and Australian plates. About 90 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous Period, the Indian Plate began moving north at 15 cm/year (6 in/yr). Between 50 and 55 million years ago, during the Eocene Epoch of the Cenozoic Era, it collided with Asia after moving 2,000 to 3,000 km (1,243 to 1,864 mi), moving faster than any other known plate. In 2007, German geologists found that the Indian Plate is half as thick as other former Gondwanaland plates, explaining its speed. The collision with the Eurasian Plate formed the Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas. As of 2009, the Indian Plate moves northeast at 5 cm/yr (2 in/yr), while the Eurasian Plate moves north at 2 cm/yr (0.8 in/yr), making India the "fastest continent," causing the Eurasian Plate to deform and the Indian Plate to compress at 4 cm/yr (1.6 in/yr). India can be divided into six physiographic regions: an arc of mountains including the Himalayas, Hindu Kush, and Patkai ranges that define the northern frontiers, formed by the ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, which block cold winds and facilitate monsoon winds, with rivers flowing into the Indo–Gangetic Plain. The Himalayas extend from Ladakh to Arunachal Pradesh, with peaks like Kanchenjunga (8,598 m) and Nanda Devi (7,816 m) rising above 7,000 m (23,000 ft); the snow line ranges from 6,000 m (20,000 ft) in Sikkim to 3,000 m (9,800 ft) in Ladakh. The peninsular region lies between the Western and Eastern Ghats, south of the Narmada River, and is the oldest and most stable part of India. The term "ghat" refers to a valley or a mountain pass, such as the Bhor Ghat or Charmadi Ghat, and is used to describe mountain ranges like the Western and Eastern Ghats, which are the largest in peninsular India. The Indo-Gangetic plains, also known as the Great Plains, cover 700,000 km² (270,000 sq mi), run parallel to the Himalayas from Jammu and Kashmir to Assam, and are dominated by the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra rivers and their tributaries including the Yamuna, Chambal, Gomti, Ghaghara, Kosi, Sutlej, Ravi, Beas, Chenab, and Tista, as well as the Meghna in the Ganges Delta. The plains are flat, conducive to irrigation, rich in groundwater, and one of the world's most intensely farmed areas, primarily growing rice and wheat in rotation, with maize, sugarcane, and cotton also cultivated. The region is among the world's most densely populated. The Thar Desert, considered the seventh or tenth largest in the world, covers 200,000 to 238,700 km² (77,200 to 92,200 sq mi), mostly in Rajasthan (61% of its area), with about 10% sand dunes and 90% craggy rock, compacted salt-lake bottoms, and fixed dunes. Annual temperatures range from 0°C (32°F) in winter to over 50°C (122°F) in summer; rainfall is limited to 100–500 mm (3.9–19.7 in) during the July–September monsoon, with water at depths of 30 to 120 metres (98 to 394 ft). Rainfall varies from below 120 mm (4.7 in) in the west to 375 mm (14.8 in) in the east. The only river in the region is the Luni. Soils are sandy to sandy-loam, with variable consistency and depth. The Kutch region in Gujarat and Koyna in Maharashtra are classified as high-risk earthquake zones; Bhuj was the epicenter of the 2001 Gujarat earthquake, which killed over 1,337 people and injured 166,836, destroying nearly a million homes; the 1993 Latur earthquake killed 7,928 and injured 30,000. Other areas have moderate to low earthquake risk. The Eastern Coastal Plain stretches from Tamil Nadu to West Bengal, between the Eastern Ghats and the ocean, drained by the Mahanadi, Godavari, Kaveri, and Krishna rivers. It receives both northeast and southwest monsoon rains, with annual rainfall averaging 1,000 to 3,000 mm (39 to 118 in), and varies between 100 and 130 km (62 to 81 mi) in width. The Western Coastal Plain is a narrow strip between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, ranging from 50 to 100 km (31 to 62 mi) in width, extending from Gujarat through Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, and Kerala. Rivers like the Tapti, Narmada, Mandovi, and Zuari originate in the Western Ghats and flow into estuaries. The region has deciduous vegetation, with the Malabar Coast moist forests forming a unique ecoregion. The Western Coastal Plain is divided into the Konkan and Malabar Coast. The Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands are India's two major island formations and are classified as union territories. The Lakshadweep Islands lie 200 to 440 km (120 to 270 mi) off Kerala in the Arabian Sea, consisting of twelve atolls, three reefs, and five submerged banks, with about 35 islands and islets and a total area of 32 km² (12 sq mi). The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are located between 6° and 14° north latitude and 92° and 94° east longitude, comprising 572 islands in a north–south axis of approximately 910 km, located 1,255 km (780 mi) from Kolkata and 193 km (120 mi) from Cape Negrais in Burma. The territory includes two groups: the Andaman Islands (325 islands, 6,170 km²) and the Nicobar Islands (247 islands, 1,765 km²). India's only active volcano, Barren Island, is located here and last erupted in 2017.

The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie between 6° and 14° north latitude and 92° and 94° east longitude, consisting of 572 islands arranged in a north–south axis for approximately 910 km in the Bay of Bengal near the Myanmar coast. They are located 1,255 km (780 mi) from Kolkata (Calcutta) and 193 km (120 mi) from Cape Negrais in Burma. The territory includes two island groups: the Andaman Islands with 325 islands covering 6,170 km² (2,380 sq mi) and the Nicobar Islands with 247 islands covering 1,765 km² (681 sq mi). India's only active volcano, Barren Island, is situated here and last erupted in 2017; there is also a dormant volcano named Narcondum and a mud volcano at Baratang. Indira Point, India's southernmost land point, is located in the Nicobar Islands at 6°45’10″N and 93°49’36″E, lying just 189 km (117 mi) from Sumatra, Indonesia, and the highest point is Mount Thullier at 642 m (2,106 ft). Other significant Indian islands include Diu, a former Portuguese colony; Majuli, a river island of the Brahmaputra; Elephanta in Bombay Harbour; and Sriharikota, a barrier island in Andhra Pradesh. Salsette Island is India's most populous island, hosting the city of Mumbai (Bombay). Forty-two islands in the Gulf of Kutch form the Marine National Park. India's major resource-based industries are fisheries, agriculture, mining, and petroleum products. It has the 18th-largest exclusive economic zone (EEZ) globally, measuring 2,305,143 km² (890,021 sq mi), which includes the Lakshadweep island group in the Laccadive Sea and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. India was ranked seventh among countries most affected by climate change in 2019. Rising temperatures on the Tibetan Plateau are causing Himalayan glaciers to retreat, threatening the flow of the Ganges, Brahmaputra, Indus, Yamuna, and other major rivers; a 2007 WWF report indicated the Indus River may run dry for this reason. Severe landslides and floods are projected to increase in states like Assam. India's temperatures have risen by 0.7 °C (1.3 °F) between 1901 and 2018, and projections suggest droughts will become more frequent and severe by the end of the century. Ecological disasters, such as the 1998 coral bleaching event that killed over 70% of corals in Lakshadweep and Andaman reefs due to elevated ocean temperatures from global warming, are expected to become more common. India has about 14,500 km of inland navigable waterways and twelve major rivers with a total catchment area exceeding 2,528,000 km² (976,000 sq mi). All major rivers originate from three main watersheds: the Himalayan river networks, which are snow-fed and perennial, and two monsoon-dependent systems. The Himalayan rivers flowing westward into Punjab are the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej. The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghana system has the largest catchment area of about 1,600,000 km² (620,000 sq mi), with the Ganges Basin alone covering about 1,100,000 km² (420,000 sq mi); the Ganges originates from the Gangotri Glacier in Uttarakhand, flows southeast into the Bay of Bengal, and is joined by the Yamuna and Gomti rivers in the plains. The Brahmaputra begins in Tibet, China, as the Yarlung Tsangpo River, enters India in Arunachal Pradesh, flows west through Assam, and merges with the Ganges in Bangladesh as the Jamuna River. The Chambal, a tributary of the Ganges via the Yamuna, originates from the Vindhya-Satpura watershed; the Narmada and Tapi rivers, also from this watershed, flow west into the Arabian Sea in Gujarat. The Deccan rivers, originating from the Western Ghats and including the Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri, drain into the Bay of Bengal and constitute 20% of India's total outflow. Heavy southwest monsoon rains cause the Brahmaputra and other rivers to overflow, flooding surrounding areas, which provide irrigation for rice farmers but have killed thousands and displaced populations. Major gulfs include the Gulf of Cambay, Gulf of Kutch, and Gulf of Mannar; key straits are the Palk Strait (separating India from Sri Lanka), the Ten Degree Channel (separating the Andamans from the Nicobars), and the Eight Degree Channel (separating the Laccadive and Amindivi Islands from Minicoy). Important capes include Kanyakumari (formerly Cape Comorin), the southern tip of mainland India; Indira Point, the southernmost point in India; Rama's Bridge, and Point Calimere. The Arabian Sea lies to the west, the Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean to the east and south, respectively. Smaller seas include the Laccadive Sea and the Andaman Sea. India has four coral reefs: in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep, and Gulf of Kutch. Key lakes include Sambhar Lake (largest saltwater lake in Rajasthan), Vembanad Lake (Kerala), Kolleru Lake (Andhra Pradesh), Loktak Lake (Manipur), Dal Lake (Kashmir), Chilka Lake (Odisha), and Sasthamkotta Lake (Kerala). India's wetland ecosystem spans from the cold, arid regions of Ladakh to the humid peninsular areas, most linked to river networks. The government has identified 71 wetlands for conservation within sanctuaries and national parks. Mangrove forests are widespread along the Indian coastline in estuaries, creeks, backwaters, salt marshes, and mudflats, covering a total of 4,461 km² (1,722 mi²), which is 7% of the world's total mangrove cover. Prominent mangrove areas are in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Sundarbans delta, the Gulf of Kutch, and the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, and Krishna rivers; large mangrove areas also exist in parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Kerala. The Sundarbans delta, at the mouth of the Ganges, spans across Bangladesh and West Bengal and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized separately as Sundarbans (Bangladesh) and Sundarbans National Park (India). It features a complex network of tidal waterways, mudflats, and salt-tolerant mangrove forests, supporting diverse fauna including birds, spotted deer, crocodiles, snakes, and the Bengal tiger—estimated at 400 individuals and about 30,000 spotted deer. The Rann of Kutch, a marshy region in northwestern Gujarat and bordering Pakistan, covers 27,900 km² (10,800 sq mi), originally part of the Arabian Sea, now a seasonal salt marsh due to geological forces like earthquakes and silt accumulation, flooding to knee-depth during monsoons and drying afterward. India's arable land area of 1,597,000 km² (394.6 million acres) is the second largest globally, after the United States, with a gross irrigated crop area of 826,000 km² (215.6 million acres), the largest in the world, followed by the US and China. Of the 160 million hectares of cultivated land, 39 million hectares are irrigated by groundwater wells and 22 million by canals. In 2010, only 35% of agricultural land was reliably irrigated, and about two-thirds of cultivated land depends on monsoons. India is the world's largest producer of mica blocks and splittings, second-largest producer of barite and chromite, third-largest coal producer, fourth in iron ore production, fifth in bauxite, second in crude steel (as of February 2018), seventh in manganese ore, and eighth in aluminium. India has significant sources of titanium ore, diamonds, and limestone and possesses 24% of the world's known and economically viable thorium, mined along Kerala's shores. Gold was mined in the now-defunct Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka. India's total renewable water resources are estimated at 1,907.8 km³ annually, with usable and replenishable groundwater at 350 billion cubic metres; only 35% of groundwater is currently utilized. About 44 million tonnes of cargo move annually through India's major rivers and waterways. Groundwater supplies 40% of water in irrigation canals, and 56% of land is arable and used for agriculture. Black soils, moisture-retentive and rich in clay, are preferred for dry farming and crops like cotton and linseed; forest soils are used for tea and coffee; red soils have high iron content. Most of India's estimated 5.4 billion barrels (860,000,000 m³) of oil reserves are located in the Mumbai High, upper Assam, Cambay, Krishna-Godavari, and Cauvery basins. India possesses about seventeen trillion cubic feet of natural gas in Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, and Odisha, and uranium is mined in Andhra Pradesh. India has 400 medium-to-high enthalpy thermal springs for geothermal energy in seven areas: the Himalayas, Sohana, Cambay, the Narmada-Tapti delta, the Godavari delta, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (specifically Barren Island). Based on the Köppen system, India has six major climatic subtypes, including arid deserts in the west, alpine tundra and glaciers in the north, and humid tropical regions in the southwest and island territories. The country has four seasons: winter (January–February), summer (March–May), monsoon (June–September), and post-monsoon (October–December). The Himalayas act as a barrier to frigid katabatic winds from Central Asia, keeping northern India warm in winter and relatively hot in summer. Although the Tropic of Cancer passes through India, the entire country is considered tropical. Summer lasts from March to June, with temperatures exceeding 40 °C (104 °F) in most areas and over 45 °C (113 °F) in the Thar Desert; coastal regions exceed 30 °C (86 °F) with high humidity. The southwest monsoon splits into two arms: the Bay of Bengal arm, which moves north across northeast India in early June, and the Arabian Sea arm, which deposits rain on the windward side of the Western Ghats. Winters in peninsular India have mild to warm days and cool nights, with cooler temperatures further north and some areas experiencing freezing; most of northern India faces fog. The highest recorded temperature in India was 51 °C (124 °F) in Phalodi, Rajasthan, and the lowest was −60 °C (−76 °F) in Dras, Jammu and Kashmir. India's geological features are classified by era: the Precambrian Cudappah and Vindhyan systems are spread across eastern and southern states, with small parts in western and central India; Paleozoic formations (Cambrian to Triassic) are found in the Western Himalayas; the Mesozoic Deccan Traps, formed by sub-aerial volcanic activity, cover most of northern Deccan and produce black, fertile trap soil; Tertiary imprints are in Manipur, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, and along the Himalayas; the Cretaceous system is in central India and parts of the Indo-Gangetic plains; the Gondwana system is in the Narmada River area in the Vindhyas and Satpuras; the Eocene system is in the western Himalayas and Assam; Oligocene formations are in Kutch and Assam; the Pleistocene system is in central India, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands were formed in this era by volcanoes. The Himalayas were formed by the convergence and deformation of the Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates, which continue to raise the mountain range by one centimetre annually. Indian soils are classified into eight categories: alluvial (80% of total land surface, derived from river silt in the Great Northern plains, fertile but lacking nitrogen and phosphorus), black (in Deccan lava region of Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh, high clay content and moisture retention), red (in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka plateau, Andhra plateau, Chota Nagpur plateau, and Aravallis, deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus), laterite (formed in tropical regions with heavy rainfall due to leaching, found in Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, and hilly northeastern states), forest (on mountain slopes in Himalayas, Western Ghats, and Eastern Ghats, rich in humus), arid and desert, saline and alkaline, and peaty and organic soils. The National Disaster Management Authority states that 60% of Indian landmass is prone to earthquakes and 8% is susceptible to cyclone risks. Cratons are continental crust composed of a platform and basement layer; a shield is where basement rock is exposed at the surface.

The National Disaster Management Authority states that 60% of India's land area is susceptible to earthquakes and 8% is at risk from cyclones. Black soils are well developed in the Deccan lava region of Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh, containing a high percentage of clay and being moisture retentive. Red soils are present in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka plateau, Andhra plateau, Chota Nagpur plateau, and the Aravallis, and are deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus. Laterite soils form in tropical areas with heavy rainfall, where leaching removes soluble materials from the topsoil, and are typically found in the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, and hilly regions of the northeastern states with heavy rainfall. Forest soils occur on mountain and hill slopes in the Himalayas, Western Ghats, and Eastern Ghats, and are characterized by large amounts of dead leaves and organic matter known as humus. Cratons are a type of continental crust composed of a top platform layer and an older basement layer. A shield is the portion of a craton where the basement rock is exposed at the surface and is considered the older, more stable region, largely unaffected by plate tectonic activity. The Indian Craton is divided into five major cratons.
